content:
The new land title registration system will be implemented in the first half of next year,the government has also tightened the existing land search arrangements, requiring that searches must meet one of nine "specified purposes". News purposes are not listed; applications can only be made on grounds of "public interest", and applicants must declare that the search records will be used solely for the declared purpose and explain how the records will be used to achieve that purpose. Applications will be considered by the Land Registrar on a "case-by-case basis"; if the Registrar is not satisfied, the application must be refused, and false or misleading statements will attract criminal liability. The subsidiary legislation was gazetted last Friday (the 16th) under the "enact-then-review" procedure, and will be scrutinised by the Legislative Council tomorrow (the 21st).

Under the current land deeds registration system, there are no restrictions on who may search land records. Section 21 of the Land Registration Regulations merely states that upon receiving a request from any person together with payment of the prescribed fee, the Land Registrar must provide the records as soon as practicable.

Government: citing other departments' practices

The government gazetted eight pieces of subsidiary legislation on the new land title registration system last Friday (the 16th), proposing to restrict search arrangements for both lands under the existing Land Registration Ordinance and new lands, requiring that searches must meet one of nine "specified purposes". The authorities said the review was conducted by reference to the relevant practices of other government departments, and that the measures aim to strike a balance between safeguarding personal data privacy and maintaining the role and function of the Land Registry's search system to ensure transparency and efficiency, describing these as vital to the operation of Hong Kong's property market and economy.

The "specified purposes" include facilitating the disposition of registered interests, due diligence such as property valuation, building management, market research and so on. Purposes relating to news reporting are not listed; only one item refers to "searching or inspecting records in furtherance of the public interest". On what constitutes "public interest", a footnote in the document gives the example that in news investigations involving large-scale unauthorised building works and ownerless properties, it is necessary to apply to search the relevant property's land records. For applications made on this ground, the applicant must provide a declaration stating that the land records sought are required for the declared purpose and will be used only for that purpose, and explaining how the records will be used to achieve the declared purpose. If the Registrar is not satisfied of the application purpose, the application must be refused. The document does not specify whether an appeal mechanism has been put in place.

The authorities said the Registrar will "consider each case individually" for public interest applications. Factors to be considered include, but are not limited to, the purpose of the search, whether the public interest involved in disclosure outweighs the owner's privacy, how the records will be used to serve the public interest, and whether they may be misused or abused. However, these factors are not set out in the provisions of the subsidiary legislation. The authorities also said that further details of the search arrangements will be set out in guidelines to be issued by the Land Registry.

Offenders liable on conviction to a fine of HK$10,000 and imprisonment for six months

Furthermore, under the amended Land Registration Regulations, the Registrar may require an applicant to provide any information, documents, confirmations or declarations that the Registrar considers necessary for the application, and may specify the scope and manner in which the registered records are to be provided. Any person who knowingly or recklessly makes a false or misleading statement on a material particular commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine of HK$10,000 and imprisonment for six months.

According to records, in July this year the authorities stated that the "initial concept" of "specified purposes" included "conducting market surveys or making reports on the property market". In this gazettal, it has been changed to "conducting research or general analysis for academic purposes or for reporting on the property market". Comparing the two, the Chinese version no longer contains the words "survey" or "report", while the English version retains "research" and "reporting", but the Chinese version adopts the terms "research" and "report".

Moreover, under the new title registration system, the authorities said "historical records" include registration application forms for past property transfers and documents relating to building orders that have already been complied with. As these contain sensitive personal data and may not have a direct bearing on title verification under the new system, they may be accessed only by "specified persons", namely parties to the records, professionals, and persons who declare that the application is made to search records in the public interest.

Native researcher Chan Kim-ching: caring about community development should not require proving public interest　

The Local Research Institute has previously conducted land searches for research into developers hoarding land, occupying land and unauthorised building works. Researcher Chan Kim-ching said he did not mind having to state the purpose of the search application, but was concerned about the criteria and time required for the authorities' consideration, worrying that if the process drags on for two or three months, the media may not be able to follow up on public interest issues in a timely manner. "(If) you delay it to the point where something truly in the public interest is prevented from being achieved, that in fact affects the public's understanding of the problem. I think this is the biggest issue."

Chan also explained that investigation or research is itself a process, and it is common for research findings to differ from the original intent—for example, an investigation into unauthorised building works may later uncover building safety issues. He therefore worried about whether, if the research results do not align with the declared purpose, this could constitute a false or misleading statement. He also considered it "very uneconomical" for the authorities to have to devote additional procedures and costs to such consideration under the amended legislation.

Chan Kim-ching pointed out that while certain land records do involve personal data privacy, information such as who holds a piece of land and what changes have been made to it is of a public nature, and may even be accessed free of charge in other countries. He gave the example that if the public wants to know whether a community has been acquired by a certain developer or is concerned about community development, they should not have to make an additional effort to prove that this serves the public interest. Among the current nine specified purposes, apart from public interest, there is also "conducting research or general analysis for academic purposes or for reporting on the property market". Chan said that the actual operation would need to be tested in due course, and expressed hope that the authorities would provide clear and explicit criteria for "public interest" and set a time limit for consideration.

After losing the vehicle plate search case, the Transport Department tightens search arrangements

In recent years, the government has repeatedly tightened media search arrangements. As early as November 2021, the Companies Registry and the Land Registry already required searches to be conducted in the applicants' real names. Tsoi Yuk-ling, a former producer-director of RTHK's "Kai Song Kei" (Hong Kong Connection) was charged with making a false statement after selecting "other matters relating to traffic and transport" as the purpose of her search while investigating the 7.21 incident. The case ended in an ultimate victory in June 2023, with the judge ruling that the Transport Department had no reason to exclude bona fide news investigations. However, in January of the following year, the Transport Department tightened vehicle registration mark searches. For news-related or other reasons, searches of vehicle plates can only be applied for as an "exceptional case", subject to vetting by the Commissioner for Transport, and will be approved only when the public interest outweighs the vehicle owner's right to privacy. Applications that would be detrimental to national security will be rejected., the Transport Department tightened vehicle registration mark searches in January of the following year, requiring that for news-related or other reasons, searches of vehicle plates can only be applied for as an "exceptional case", subject to vetting by the Commissioner for Transport, and will be approved only when the public interest outweighs the vehicle owner's right to privacy. Applications that would be detrimental to national security will be rejected.

The Hong Kong Journalists Association filed a judicial review,which was rejected by the High Court in March this year. The judge held that the policy did not "across the board" refuse all applications made for news purposes and did not disproportionately restrict press freedom. The HKJA expressed regret at the ruling, pointing out that of the 17 news-related applications made up to the time of the judicial review, only one application was partially approved after several months, and that the judgment had not adequately taken into account the practical difficulties faced by the industry in applying.
